title: Skill Acquisition in Paralympic Sport
abstract: This chapter examines how ecological dynamics (ED) can be translated into coaching practice within high-performance Paralympic sport. While ecological dynamics offers a powerful rationale for understanding skill learning, many coaches experience difficulty operationalising its concepts in daily training. Drawing on applied work across the three-year cycle leading into the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games, this chapter illustrates how Skill Acquisition Specialists can lead the iterative and relational process of translation with coaches, rather than a linear application of theory. Five interconnected strategies are presented that were used to support coaches to engage with ED principles: reframing language, promoting live task design, iterating and experimenting, working through relationships, and reading for readiness. When applied in context, these strategies helped coaches reconceptualise performance problems, design more representative tasks, and foreground adaptability and individualisation in training environments shaped by diverse athlete impairments. A more detailed case study traces one coach's learning journey, demonstrating how ecological principles were translated to practice through co-design and interaction rather than prescriptive instruction. Persistent coaching challenges, including discomfort with less control, time constraints, and entrenched beliefs, highlight the need for scaffolding and ecosystem-level support. Overall, the chapter positions translation as a core practice of a Skill Acquisition Specialist for enabling theory to inform, shape, and enhance coaching.

title: Skill Acquisition in Climbing
abstract: In this chapter, we present a non-linear pedagogy to skill acquisition in climbing, which is underpinned by five principles anchored in ecological dynamics approach: the representativeness of the situation, focus of attention, functional variability through exploratory behaviours, manipulation of constraints, and ensuring relevant information-movement interactions (e.g., favouring perception of affordances). We explain how those principles can guide practitioners to design interventions that promote safe and effective exploration for route reading (i.e., previewing) and for sport climbing (speed, lead, and bouldering) but also for outdoor climbing.

title: Skill Acquisition in Strength & Conditioning
abstract: This chapter explores how the application of strength and conditioning (S&C) principles can regulate the acquisition of adaptable sport-specific skills. In this light, the impact of S&C on action-scaled affordances is discussed. The application of skill acquisition principles in the gym is considered, including use of the constraints-led approach and its varying effects on movement coordination across multiple timescales. The benefits of greater integration of skill acquisition principles with S&C activity design to develop more contextually relevant ‘conditioning’ tasks are also introduced. To enhance S&C coaches’ consideration of skill acquisition principles in their practice, weighted implement training is referenced as the modality has been shown to concurrently enhance general physical capacities yet degrade sport-specific skill performance, thus underlining the importance of considering perceptual-motor system (re)calibration to performance demands following S&C participation. This chapter culminates with key S&C considerations as it concerns broadening the affordance landscape and optimising training transfer.

title: Skill Acquisition in Physical Education
abstract: Following international trends in innovative and contemporary approaches to skill acquisition, Physical Education (PE) teachers are excited about the potential these methods offer for enhancing pedagogical practices. The work by Chow, Renshaw et al., and Moy et al. challenges the relevance of traditional approaches in teaching movement skills and highlights the advantages of contemporary methods in enhancing motivation to learn. Contemporary teaching methods, such as the constraints-led approach (CLA) or nonlinear pedagogy (NLP) to skill acquisition, are gaining traction among practitioners. While some professions, like sport coaching have made progress to embrace contemporary skill acquisition quickly into their practice, PE teachers may still need more support in adopting such pedagogical approaches. This chapter will provide a discussion on the theoretical framework of traditional and contemporary skill acquisition approaches, challenges in implementing a contemporary pedagogy, and a case study on how such pedagogical approaches can be implemented.

title: The Future of Skill Acquisition
abstract: The Constraints-Led Approach (CLA) posits that behaviour emerges during learning and development through various interacting constraints, allowing individuals to exploit inherent tendencies for self-organisation. This framework has garnered significant attention from academics and practitioners interested in skill acquisition. Over the past 40 years, the continued development of theory and practice associated with CLA has enhanced its engagement and application within the sport sciences. As a result, numerous national sports organisations, professional teams, and individual coaches have adopted CLA principles in practice across a diverse range of sports, including professional football, the NBA, American football, canoeing, dance, figure skating, team sports, swimming, and golf. However, this alternative approach has led to several questions for advocates and practitioners wishing to implement CLA principles. In this chapter, we explore these challenges, framing them as opportunities for practitioners interested in adopting and applying CLA principles in their own work. By embracing these challenges, practitioners can deepen their understanding of skill acquisition and enhance their effectiveness in coaching and athlete development.

title: Skill Acquisition in Sports Officiating
abstract: This chapter examines skill acquisition in sports officiating, an under-researched yet critical domain. It outlines practical frameworks to guide development across officiating roles and contexts. Critically, the chapter highlights the diversity of officiating demands, shaped by levels of interaction with athletes and coaches, physical demands, cue processing, technology use, and developmental stage. Two central challenges are identified: creating representative practice environments and effectively evaluating performance. Drawing on Ecological Dynamics and Representative Learning Design, the chapter emphasises the importance of aligning training with real-world constraints. It acknowledges the role and limitations of traditional video-based approaches and the emerging potential of immersive technologies such as virtual reality. To address these challenges, the chapter presents application of key frameworks from broader motor learning research. Specifically, the Periodization of Skill Training (PoST) and the Challenge Point Framework are adapted to officiating contexts to help optimise learning, retention, and transfer. Practical examples and a case study of an elite-level VR training system illustrate application in high-performance settings, alongside reflections on resource constraints and self-directed learning. Overall, the chapter advocates for context-sensitive, evidence-informed approaches using core skill acquisition research and knowledge to enhance the effectiveness, consistency, and long-term development of sports officials.

title: Correspondence Between Small-Sided Games Implementation and Competitive Ball Progression in Elite Football: A Retrospective Case Study
authors: I Dewa Made Arya Nanda Wijaya Kusuma
abstract: Background & objective: Small-sided games (SSGs) are widely used in football because they manipulate player numbers, playing area, rules, while preserving key features of match play. However, evidence linking SSG implementation to ball progression during elite competition remains limited when SSGs are embedded in a real-world preparation programme rather than imposed experimentally. This study examined the correspondence between SSG implementation and ball progression performance in the East Java Provincial Football Team during the 2024 National Sports Week (PON XXI). Materials & Methods: A quantitative ex post facto performance-analysis design was used. Official training documentation, match recordings, match statistics, were reviewed. The performance dataset comprised three PON matches against Papua Pegunungan, West Java, and Aceh. SSG implementation was characterised by player-number modification, playing-area manipulation, game constraints, intensity, and training objectives. Ball progression was assessed using passing accuracy, attacking-third passes, successful progressive passes, through passes, and chances created. Descriptive statistics were used because the available dataset did not support a valid participant-level inferential model. STROBE was used as the reporting framework. Results: Across the three analysed matches, possession ranged from 31% to 47% and passing accuracy from 63.46% to 72.87%. Successful progressive passes ranged from 19 to 40, successful attacking-third passes from 80 to 115, and chances created from 2 to 7. Progressive passing and through passes were present in all three matches. title: PENGEMBANGAN MODEL PEMBELAJARAN SEPAK BOLA BERBASIS TGfU MELALUI SMALL-SIDED GAMES UNTUK MENINGKATKAN KETERAMPILAN TEKNIK DAN TACTICAL AWARENESS MAHASISWA PENDIDIKAN JASMANI
abstract: Football courses in physical education study programs are still dominated by isolated technical drills, so that students master techniques in closed situations but struggle to apply them during game play. This study aimed to develop a football learning model based on Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) through small-sided games and to test its effectiveness in improving technical skills and tactical awareness. A research and development design adapted from Borg and Gall was carried out in three stages: preliminary study, model development and validation, and effectiveness testing. The model consists of six syntactical steps, namely game, game appreciation, tactical awareness, decision making, skill execution, and performance. The model was validated by three experts and tried out on 12 students. Effectiveness was tested using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design involving 56 students (28 experimental and 28 control). Data were analyzed using N-Gain, independent samples t-test, Cohen’s d, and MANOVA. The model was rated highly feasible (88.8%), with 91.7% syntax implementation and 87.4% practicality. The experimental group achieved a higher N-Gain than the control group in technical skills (0.51 vs 0.25; t = 6.47; p < 0.001; d = 1.73) and tactical awareness (0.50 vs 0.20; t = 7.98; p < 0.001; d = 2.13), with a significant simultaneous effect (Wilks’ Lambda = 0.512; F(2,53) = 25.27; p < 0.001). The model is feasible, practical, and effective, and equips prospective physical education teachers with a game-based framework that can be adapted for football lessons in elementary schools.

title: Skill Acquisition in Sport Performance Analysis and Biomechanics
abstract: This chapter explores how skill acquisition specialists can leverage performance analysis and biomechanics to optimise athlete and coach performance through evidence-based intervention design. The authors examine two approaches: notational analysis and biomechanical analysis, each capable of capturing distinct dimensions of sporting performance during training and competition. Two integrated case studies demonstrate practical application: an Australian Football intervention using notational analysis to evaluate the representativeness of small-sided games in replicating match demands, and a swimming case study employing biomechanical analysis to support technique refinement. Both exemplify how multidisciplinary teams combining skill acquisition specialists, performance analysts, and coaches can translate complex performance data into actionable training design modifications. The chapter acknowledges inherent challenges in interdisciplinary practice, including difficulties measuring subjective elements (e.g., decision-making), the time-intensive nature of post-performance analysis, and translating data complexity into meaningful coaching feedback. A coach's perspective from Australian Football contextualises how performance analysis has transformed strategic thinking and training methodology. The authors conclude that integrating performance analysis with skill acquisition principles enables teams and individuals to gain competitive advantage through optimised training design informed by both training and competition environment data.

title: Skill Acquisition in Team Sport
abstract: This chapter explains how team sport players require the ability to outwit their opponent, which is a key element of game understanding. In doing so, players require different knowledge and skills, which at the highest level involves players being strategic about what action to take next and why. Drawing from principles of video game design, the chapter introduces two different sport coaching methods: Digital Video Game Design (DVGD) and Gamification. This chapter explains how these methods have different purposes, presenting them both as viable tools for coaches to consider in team sport coaching contexts. DVGD emphasises player problem-solving skills using pedagogical principles such as superpowers, level-ups, and pauses, while Gamification promotes engaging in skill execution with challenges and rewards. Findings from applying DVGD and Gamification from a case study example in youth soccer demonstrated how individual players within the team experienced different challenges and benefits when engaging with the two named coaching methods. In summary, this chapter provides real-world insight into how team sport coaches can think critically about how to use principles of video game design in their coaching practice to enhance how players outwit their opponent, whilst appreciating there is no ‘one size fits all’ coaching method.

title: Skill Acquisition in Learning
abstract: Skilled motor performance is often described as the product of automatic processes that operate outside conscious awareness. This perspective has been particularly influential in sport psychology, where conscious control is frequently associated with performance disruption, choking under pressure, and reinvestment in movement mechanics. However, emerging theoretical and empirical work suggests that this view may be overly simplistic. Conscious processes do not disappear with expertise; rather, they change in form and function. This chapter critically examines the role of conscious control in skilled movement, drawing on research from motor learning, sport psychology, and cognitive science. We argue that conscious engagement in performance exists along a continuum, ranging from detailed movement monitoring to higher-level strategic, attentional, and reflective processes. While directing attention to specific movement mechanics can disrupt well-learned skills, other forms of conscious engagement, such as situational awareness, rhythm regulation, or tactical decision-making, may support performance and adaptability. We also discuss how individual differences, such as propensity for reinvestment, and contextual factors, such as pressure or novelty, influence when conscious control becomes helpful or harmful. Finally, we outline practical implications for coaching and training, emphasising the importance of developing athletes’ capacity to regulate conscious engagement across different stages of skill development and performance contexts rather than attempting to eliminate conscious control altogether.

title: Skill Acquisition in Practice
abstract: The role of Skill Acquisition Specialists (SAS) within high-performance sport has evolved significantly since their emergence in the early 2000s. While recent literature has attempted to define the SAS role, less attention has been paid to how their professional practice influences coach development, practice design, and athlete performance. This chapter explores SAS practice through three practitioner perspectives, highlighting decision-making as a critical pillar of effective support. Each perspective illustrates distinct approaches (e.g., professional judgment and decision-making, espoused theory/theory-in-use for guiding coach learning, and design thinking for collaborative practice design) while emphasising a coach focus that is flexible and contextually relevant. We suggest that SAS effectiveness depends not only on technical expertise but also on relational, communication, and adaptive skills that enable specialists to navigate complex, uncertain environments. A comparative analysis of these approaches reveals a spectrum of engagement styles shaped by perceived roles and aims. The chapter concludes by identifying future priorities, including refining SAS competencies, enhancing decision-making development, and optimising organisational integration. By shifting the focus from defining the role to understanding how SASs work in practice, this work contributes to exploring the impact of skill acquisition within sporting systems.

title: A History of Skill Acquisition
abstract: This chapter discusses major historical influences on the field of skill acquisition that have shaped theory and practice. An initial stimulus on skill acquisition theory was pre-scientific introspection, reflection, and debate on human identity, existence, and experience by early philosophers, intellectuals, and artists. Understanding where skill acquisition theories have emerged from, especially their distinct philosophical and meta-theoretical foundations, is essential for comparing their value for practical applications in education, therapy, training, and coaching. In skill acquisition, different theories have distinct metatheoretical roots (with distinct philosophical and scientific origins and assumptions). Applying theoretical principles in practice implies acceptance of the metatheoretical assumptions underlying a particular theory. Since metatheories have distinct assumptions and beliefs, it could be illogical and incoherent to integrate concepts, ideas, methods, and principles from different theories to apply in practice. Practitioners working in skill acquisition need to be aware of the invisible golden threads of meta-theoretical logic that need to be respected and cannot be entangled (through inter-mixing key ideas from different theories) because that could lead to incoherence in how practitioners conceptualise learners and the learning process. Arguments against uncritical integration raise serious concerns about the risks of blending ideas, concepts, and tools from distinct theories without careful consideration. These risks include using contradictory and less effective practices in the professional work of coaches, trainers, and skill acquisition specialists when intentionally selecting concepts and methods advocated in different scientific theories.

title: Experience and Implications of Japan’s Youth Football Talent Development from the Perspective of Sport–Education Integration
venue: Academic journal of management and social sciences
abstract: In April 2009, the General Administration of Sport of China, together with the Ministry of Education, issued the Notice on Launching the National Youth Campus Football Program and established the National Youth Campus Football Leading Group, thereby initiating a period of rapid development for campus football in China[1]. The General Administration of Sport’s proposed 15th Five-Year Plan regards consolidating the “three major ball sports” as a foundation for development, includes them among the revitalization objectives, and calls for continued football governance reform. Youth football should receive high priority: campus football should continue to expand; the number and quality of coaches should improve at the same time; the five-level youth training centers should develop substantially; the system of competitions should be designed around young people; a Chinese Youth Football League should be established; professional football clubs should operate in a sound manner; and professional leagues should develop healthily[2]. Japan and China are geographically close and have broadly similar population physical fitness, yet their overall football development still shows a clear gap. Japan’s rapid progress and successful rise in football are reflected not only in its higher FIFA ranking but are also closely related to its highly developed youth development system and professional leagues. Its football development did not rely on short-term campaigns; rather, it was achieved gradually through a longer-term approach and a complete system. Starting with youth development, supported by professional leagues, and using organizational development as the means, Japan ensures a continuous emergence of talent. title: Skill Acquisition in Skills Testing
abstract: Sport performance is measured most during competition where skills are deemed successful or not in the context of the game under pressure. Most assessment of such skills happens in testing conditions that do not closely reflect those competitive conditions. This chapter aims to capture the complex nature of skill assessment, shaped by the dynamic interaction between the performer and their environment, tracing its evolution from isolated, technique-focused measures to more ecologically valid approaches. We review the current state of play in skill assessment before introducing the SCORE Framework as a guide for the development and implementation of skill assessment.

title: Skill Acquisition in Esports and Gaming
abstract: This chapter examines the processes underpinning skill acquisition in Esports and video gaming. Here, we highlight how structured training methods from traditional sport can inform player development in digital performance environments. While many Esports athletes rely on repetitive grinding with limited feedback, research indicates that deliberate practice defined by structured goals, feedback, and recovery offers a more efficient route to expertise. The chapter outlines a framework that integrates cognitive and motor training with consideration for sleep, physical activity, and nutrition. It explores the importance of perceptual learning, task specificity, and environmental factors such as challenge level and team context in shaping skill development. Advances in data analytics, biofeedback, and artificial intelligence now enable highly personalised feedback loops that can optimise individual learning trajectories. Finally, emerging neurotechnologies, including brain-computer interfaces and non-invasive brain stimulation, present new opportunities for enhancing performance and accessibility in gaming. Together, these approaches position esports as a powerful model for investigating human learning, neuroplasticity, and expertise across perceptual, cognitive, and motor domains.

title: Skill Acquisition in Practice Transfer
abstract: Effective skill acquisition in high-performance sport depends not only on what athletes practice, but how practice demands are scheduled over time. This chapter examines practice scheduling as a central mechanism for supporting learning, individualization, and transfer to competition. Drawing on contemporary frameworks including Skill Acquisition Periodization, the Challenge Point framework, and the Holistic Workload approach, the chapter explores how challenge, fidelity, and load function as core design constructs in structuring practice environments. The chapter highlights the inherent uncertainty coaches face when balancing long-term development with short-term performance pressures, particularly in team settings where individual needs vary and training time is shared. It discusses how advances in measurement, analytics, and technology can help practitioners better monitor athlete responses, adjust task difficulty, and manage physical and cognitive demands across training cycles. By integrating theory with applied examples and emerging data-driven approaches, the chapter provides a practical lens for understanding how practice can be planned, adapted, and evaluated to enhance learning and support sustainable performance.

title: Carrying the Conversation Forward
abstract: This epilogue considers the future of skill acquisition as a developing applied profession. It reflects on the progress of the field, including the growing recognition of skill acquisition within sport science, the emergence of specialist roles, and the development of accreditation pathways. At the same time, it acknowledges important tensions, including limitations in the current evidence base, debates about professionalisation, and the need to clarify the distinctive contribution of the Skill Acquisition Specialist. Rather than presenting these challenges as barriers, the chapter frames them as signs of a maturing field. It argues that the future of skill acquisition will depend on stronger partnerships between researchers, practitioners, coaches, athletes, educators, and sport science professionals across domains. This chapter offers a call to action: to build a profession that is rigorous, context-sensitive, collaborative, and adaptable, while remaining focused on improving learning, practice, and performance in the environments where skill is developed and expressed.

title: Prologue
abstract: This prologue introduces Skill Acquisition in Action as an invitation to explore how skill acquisition can inform learning, practice, performance, and development across a wide range of domains. Bringing together contributions from more than 70 authors across the globe, the book positions skill acquisition not as a fixed set of answers, but as a way of asking better questions about how people learn, adapt, and perform. The chapter outlines skill acquisition as the science of practice, play, and learning environments, showing its relevance to sport, occupational performance, rehabilitation, fundamental movement, medicine, music, theatre, policing, water safety, and beyond. It also introduces the structure of the book and its emphasis on applied interpretation, collaboration, and openness across disciplines. In doing so, the prologue opens a conversation about how skill acquisition can develop in broad and meaningful ways for many, rather than narrowly for a few.

title: Skill Acquisition in Racquet Sports
abstract: This chapter offers an overview of the main theoretical and practical issues related to skill acquisition in racquet sports. It delves into the progression of different instructional approaches considering contemporary research on practice structure and methods, task design, communication and feedback mechanisms, and tactical, technical, physical, and psychological skills and processes. Additionally, the chapter discusses how individual differences and technological advancements shape skill learning strategies. Dissecting the unique demands and learning processes specific to racquet sports provides invaluable insights for researchers, coaches, and practitioners seeking to increase their understanding, optimize their training methods, and elevate their players’ overall enjoyment and competitive edge. This chapter serves as a comprehensive guide for understanding and applying skill acquisition principles in the context of racquet sports.

title: Skill Acquisition in Striking And Fielding Sports
abstract: In this chapter, I explore how key findings from skill acquisition research can be applied to developing hitting and fielding skills. Topics included are training to improve the pickup of visual information (i.e., education of attention), training gaze behavior, learning the movements involved in hitting and catch, and training to increase action capacity (e.g., running speed, lateral movement).

title: Associations between accumulated weekly external load and technical match actions in elite soccer
abstract: This study investigated the associations between accumulated weekly external load metrics and match technical performance in elite male players.19 outfield players from a Brazilian first-division club (25.7 ± 3.9 years; 80.4 ± 6.6 kg; 181.3 ± 6.7 cm) were monitored across 208 sessions (170 training sessions and 38 official matches) during a full competitive season.External load was quantified, capturing total distance (TD), PlayerLoad (PL), high-speed running distance (HSRD), total accelerations (ACC), and repeated high-intensity efforts (RHIE).Match technical performance was categorized into defensive and offensive indicators.Results showed several negative associations between accumulated weekly external load and technical performance indicators.TD was negatively associated with Clearances (β = -0.310)and Successful Forward Passes (β = -0.213),while PL was negatively associated with Clearances (β = -0.315)and Aerial Duels Won (β = -0.216).Additionally, HSRD and RHIE were negatively associated with Interceptions (β = -0.273;β = -0.284).Finally, ACC was negatively associated with Interceptions (β = -0.241),Offensive Volume (β = -0.220),and Successful Total Passes (β = -0.207).These results suggest that weeks characterized by higher training volumes and intensities may negatively affect offensive and defensive technical performance in subsequent matches.Consequently, coaches should consider the adequacy of the weekly load composition, specifically managing neuromuscular stress and exposure to high intensity before matches, to balance offensive readiness with technical precision and defensive efficiency.An integrated approach combining external load and technical-tactical monitoring can optimize training prescription and help maintain performance throughout the competitiv

title: Advances in the application of wearable inertial sensors in swimming performance analysis: a systematic review
abstract: Wearable inertial sensors, especially inertial measurement units (IMUs), are increasingly used in swimming performance analysis because they provide objective and practical monitoring in aquatic settings.This systematic review summarised recent progress in their use for swimming performance analysis, focusing on sensor configuration, outcome types, validation methods, and methodological quality.We searched Web of Science, EBSCOhost, IEEE, and PubMed for studies published in English between January 2020 and February 2026.Eligible studies involved competitive swimmers and used wearable inertial sensors during swimming to assess performance or technique outcomes.We extracted study design, participant characteristics, sensor placement, device setup, swimming tasks, outcome measures, and reference systems.Methodological quality was assessed using an adapted COSMIN Risk of Bias checklist focused on device-relevant measurement properties.A total of 21 studies met the inclusion criteria.Most were conducted in swimming pools and focused on front crawl.The sacrum or lower trunk was the most common sensor attachment site, particularly for lap segmentation, swimming velocity, and stroke cycle variables.Configurations with multiple sensors were used more often for detailed assessments of stroke timing, coordination, breathing synchronisation, and body rotation.Evidence was strongest for free-swimming outcomes, especially instantaneous velocity, lap time, stroke rate, stroke count, and related stroke cycle measures.Fewer studies addressed starts, turns, and other specific swimming phases.Overall, wearable inertial sensors appear to be capable tools for swimming performance analysis, but further research is needed to improve methodological consistency and strengthen validation across

title: The complexity of expertise, privatisation, and outsourcing in Irish Physical Education
Coach-led questioning and tactical decision-making in youth soccer, basketball, and volleyball: proposed cognitive pathways and contextual boundaries
abstract: Coach-led questioning is widely advocated in game-based training for youth soccer, basketball, and volleyball, yet its implications for tactical decision-making and cognitive load remain uncertain. This mini review critically integrates coaching observations, instructional contrasts, and adjacent cognitive studies to examine whether questions provide cognitive scaffolding or competing processing demands under differing expertise, task constraints, and timing. A meta-analysis of game-based approaches (28 studies; 1,600 participants overall) reported an 11.41-percentage-point advantage in decision-making (95% CI 4.39–18.43), based on 17 contributing studies, but did not isolate questioning. Observations of 19 youth soccer coaches recorded 71 questions per session on average, with only 7% of divergent prompts explicitly asking players to solve problems. In a school basketball comparison ( n = 37), post-test appropriate decision scores favored questioning over prescriptive feedback for passing (0.900 vs. 0.823; p = 0.026) and shooting (0.958 vs. 0.801; p = 0.003). Across these studies, instructional components frequently co-varied, limiting attribution to questioning and leaving cognitive-load mediation untested. We propose potentially co-occurring attentional scaffolding and verbal-processing competition, and recommend trials independently manipulating question content and timing while measuring cognitive processing and delayed game transfer.

title: Sensitivity of L-DED melt-pool descriptors to point-cloud representation and gradient reconstruction
abstract: Laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) simulations often export melt-pool fields as unstructured point clouds. These fields contain rich transport information, but they do not automatically provide reproducible evidence across process conditions. Coordinate duplication, irregular sampling, local gradient reconstruction, threshold selection, and region masking can each alter the apparent flow topology. We analysed 30 exports spanning six powers (200–450 W) and five late-time snapshots to determine which thermal and flow descriptors were preserved across coordinate aggregation, time, and weighted least-squares design. Direct temperature, temperature-gradient, and velocity descriptors were separated from reconstructed Q , λ 2 , and Ω N fields. At 0.70 s, the sampled powers showed different thermal and velocity patterns, but no power met all predefined temporal criteria. The 350 W maximum-velocity contrast arose from three coordinates within central distributions that overlapped the 400 W distribution. Equal-weight reconstruction recovered affine manufactured fields to numerical precision, whereas nonlinear recovery remained scale- and weighting-dependent. The reconstructed tensor descriptors therefore yielded no comparative topology conclusion. These findings show that point-cloud representation and gradient reconstruction materially constrain the interpretation of solver-exported melt-pool fields; physical fidelity against experiment, a continuous power response, and a physical mechanism remain outside the scope of the present data.

title: Exploring barriers and facilitators to Hepatitis C virus treatment access in Los Angeles County: A mixed-methods study
abstract: Diagnosed but untreated chronic Hepatitis C virus infection remains an important public health problem in Los Angeles County, particularly affecting underserved and minority groups. This mixed-methods study (October 2024-January 2025) aimed to identify and describe the barriers and facilitators to accessing Hepatitis C virus treatment among Los Angeles County residents. The study used de-identified programmatic data from 344 case-residents in a linkage-to-cure program and conducted thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with ten participants (seven untreated, three treated) from the linkage-to-cure program. Overall, 54% of case-residents reported experiencing barriers. Among those reporting specific barriers (n = 91), personal barriers were most common (43%), followed by provider-related barriers (31%), insurance barriers (13%), and inadequate access to medical care (13%). Interviews provided further context. Themes identified included homelessness, incarceration, and drug addiction as key personal barriers. Provider-related barriers included language barriers, expressed frustration in navigating the healthcare system, long wait times to see a provider, and participants’ lack of HCV information. Insurance barriers were characterized by cost barriers and inadequate access to medical care due to a lack of transportation. Facilitators of treatment access included personal motivation to seek treatment, family and community-based support systems, trust in their medical provider, adequate insurance coverage, understanding the benefits of HCV treatment, and the desire to avoid stigmatization. title: A Narrative Review of Sport Specific Focus of Attention Instructions on Athlete Sport Skill Performance.
abstract: The purpose of the present narrative review was to synthesize the available findings from research examining sport specific focus of attention instructions on the performance of Tier 3 and Tier 4 athletes on sport specific motor tasks. Thirteen empirical studies were identified as meeting the eligibility criteria for this narrative review. Our review of the research showed mixed support for an advantage of an external focus of attention for the performance of sport specific skills, independent of the classification of the motor task (i.e. discrete or continuous). The remaining research reviewed showed motor performance was similar for the athletes when provided external or internal focus of attention instructions. These findings, together with recent concerns regarding reporting bias in the broader focus-of-attention literature, suggest that claims regarding the consistent superiority of an external focus should be interpreted cautiously. The findings from our review highlighted the impact of task relevant content in modulating the effectiveness of the instructional statements, and the importance of providing the athlete control over the focus of attention instructions. There was limited theoretical interpretation of findings when motor performance was similar for internal and external focus of attention instructions. Evidence-based practical implications are suggested for the coach and athlete.

title: A multi-mechanism partial counterbalancing approach for multi-session esports performance research in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive.
abstract: Esports performance research increasingly relies on repeated-measures designs, in which each player serves as their own control. Such designs are efficient, but they are vulnerable to order effects: participants improve with practice, tire within a session, and carry the influence of one condition into the next. Competitive gaming makes this problem unusually acute, because skill acquisition in digital games is rapid and session fatigue develops quickly. The conventional remedy, complete counterbalancing, is unattainable once a study tests more than a handful of conditions. This article describes and evaluates a partial counterbalancing strategy that layers four mechanisms: category-level Latin square sequencing, randomisation of values within categories, forward-reverse distribution of sequences across participants, and temporal spacing with session truncation. The strategy was implemented in an 18-week laboratory study of 170 South African Counter-Strike: Global Offensive players, testing six categories of hardware and in-game settings at three values each. Three independent checks were used to evaluate whether order effects had been controlled. Conditions were evenly distributed across testing positions in every setting category. Performance at the first testing position did not differ from performance at later positions on any of five metrics, with all effect sizes below the threshold for a small effect. Adding order covariates to the study's primary analyses did not reverse the direction of any effect, and left the great majority essentially unchanged; a small number of effects involving kill and death counts lost significance once order was controlled, and are identified as requiring additional care. The contribution is a transparent, auditable worked example rath

title: Goalkeeper coaches' decision-making in back-pass situations: comparing 2D, video, and immersive virtual reality perspectives
abstract: Section: Preprints Categories: Coaching, Sport Psychology, Motor Control, Learning, and Behavior Keywords: decision making, Football, virtual reality, perceptual cognitive, Visual exploratory activity, goalkeeper In modern football, goalkeepers play an increasingly central role in build-up play, requiring advanced perceptual–cognitive skills to manage back-pass situations. While decision-making and visual exploratory activity (VEA) have been widely studied in outfield players, goalkeeper-specific evidence remains limited, particularly in immersive virtual reality (VR) environments. This study examined whether immersive VR preserves the consistency of expert goalkeeper coaches' decision-making compared with traditional visualization modalities (2D overhead and broadcast video), and whether VEA in VR predicts decision consistency. Thirty-three expert goalkeeper coaches evaluated back-pass situations across three visualization conditions (2D, video, VR) and two game plans (Maintain Possession, Advance Play). Decision selection, inter- and intra-rater agreement were recorded. Inter-rater agreement was comparable across visualization modalities for both Maintain Possession (α=0.54 to 0.60) and Advance Play decisions (α=0.39 to 0.42), with no significant between-condition differences. Importantly, higher VEA in VR predicted greater alignment with peer expert consensus for Advance Play decisions and higher VEA was significantly but weakly correlated with intra-rater decision consistency for both Maintain Possession and Advance Play decisions. These findings suggest that immersive VR preserves expert decision structures while promoting active information-seeking behaviors that become decision-critical under high tactical complexity.

title: A new foundation: Briggs takes charge of Arcadia Basketball - Your Valley
